findings.where: King and the Clergymen of Birmingham, paragraph 1: 'and urged Black citizens to withdraw their support and press their grievances in the courts instead.'
findings.problem: (c) The essay narrows what the statement asked for. 'A Call for Unity' reads: 'When rights are consistently denied, a cause should be pressed in the courts and in negotiations among local leaders, and not in the streets.' A search in this run on that exact phrase returned Wikipedia's 'A Call for Unity' and the dbu.edu text of the statement, with the summary that the signers urged 'local negotiations and court remedies'. Ledger line 169 also records 'legal channels and local negotiations'. Dropping the negotiations makes the eight look narrower than they were, in a paragraph whose point is that they were not firebrands. Ledger-only problem: the closing run's support on lines 168 and 169, 'properly pursued in the courts', is the statement's recap of the January appeal, not the April request.
findings.fix: Replace the old text 'and urged Black citizens to withdraw their support and press their grievances in the courts instead.' with: 'and urged Black citizens to withdraw their support and press their grievances in the courts and in negotiations among local leaders instead.' In ledger line 169, cite the statement's own sentence ('pressed in the courts and in negotiations among local leaders, and not in the streets') in place of 'properly pursued in the courts'.

findings.problem: (c)/(d) This paraphrase without quotation marks turns King's 'great' into 'greatest'. The sense holds, but the superlative is the essay's, not King's.
findings.fix: Replace the old text 'he had nearly concluded that the greatest obstacle to Black freedom was not the open segregationist but the white moderate,' with: 'he had nearly concluded that the great stumbling block to Black freedom was not the open segregationist but the white moderate,'

findings.where: Augustine and the Peace of Babylon, paragraph 1: 'Rome had fallen, they said, because it had abandoned its gods.'
findings.problem: Ambiguous chronology, one of the AI tells in BRIEF.md. The paragraph correctly says Rome was sacked in 410, but 'Rome had fallen' reads like the fall of the Western empire, which came 66 years later. The ledger's source (City of God Book 1's argument, line 130) speaks of 'the recent sack of Rome by the Goths'.
findings.fix: Replace the old text 'Rome had fallen, they said, because it had abandoned its gods.' with: 'Rome had been taken, they said, because it had abandoned its gods.'
